headline: A dry Friday gives way to faster-arriving tropical rain, gusty winds and localized flooding concerns this weekend
disclaimer: Independent amateur analysis. This is not an official forecast or warning. Follow the National Weather Service and local authorities during hazardous weather.

refresh.workflow: Update and commit forecast.json once. GitHub Actions automatically locks the prior issue in forecast-history.json. Then verify the GitHub Pages URL; every Google Sites embed reads the same file and refreshes automatically.

kentucky.name: Central Kentucky
kentucky.subtitle: Danville primary · Lexington comparison
kentucky.summary: Central Kentucky remains dry and warm today before the remnants of Hurricane Isaias spread rain north Saturday. The latest guidance is 6–12 hours faster than yesterday, bringing a cooler Saturday and increasing confidence in widespread Saturday-night rain. Rain and embedded thunderstorms continue Sunday before ending Sunday evening.

days.label: Friday
days.hazard: No official NWS alerts; afternoon relative humidity around 20–30% keeps fine fuels unusually dry before the weekend rain
days.forecast: Mostly sunny and warm with light east to southeast winds. Most locations reach the lower 80s, with a few warmer spots near the middle 80s. High clouds thicken during the afternoon and evening, but measurable rain should hold off through tonight.

days.label: Saturday
days.hazard: No official NWS alerts at issuance; independent analysis identifies heavy rain, localized minor flooding and east-to-southeast gusts of 30–35 mph, with isolated 40 mph gusts possible in exposed southern locations
days.forecast: Clouds thicken quickly, with rain chances increasing from south to north from late morning into early afternoon. Earlier rain would hold highs near 60, while a slower arrival could permit upper 60s or lower 70s. Rain becomes widespread and occasionally heavy Saturday evening and night, accompanied by strengthening east to southeast winds.

days.label: Sunday
days.precipitation: 80–95% during the day; decreasing to 50–70% early Sunday evening
days.hazard: No official NWS alerts at issuance; heavy rain, ponding or localized minor flooding and gusty winds remain possible, while the tornado risk is very low because surface instability should stay limited
days.forecast: Rain and embedded thunderstorms continue as the remnant circulation crosses the Ohio Valley. Weekend rainfall should generally total 0.75–1.50 inches, with localized amounts near 2.5–3 inches possible. Rain and wind diminish from west to east during the afternoon and evening, followed by drier conditions late Sunday night.

kentucky.bottomLine: Today is the final dry and warm day. Rain develops Saturday and becomes widespread Saturday night through much of Sunday. Heavy rain and gusty winds are the main concerns, but dry antecedent conditions should limit flooding to localized problem spots.
kentucky.confidence: High on today's dry warmth and widespread weekend rain; moderate on Saturday and Sunday highs because rain timing and system speed control temperatures; moderate on localized rainfall maxima and peak wind gusts

upstate.name: Upstate South Carolina
upstate.subtitle: Clemson / Central primary · Tempest excluded
upstate.summary: A dry cold-air-damming wedge makes today cloudy and near normal. Rain now appears likely to begin after midnight and becomes widespread Saturday, with the heaviest rain and greatest localized flash-flooding concern Saturday afternoon through Sunday morning. Rain exits more quickly Sunday, but a small conditional severe-weather risk may develop as the wedge erodes.

currentConditions.condition: Network observations are WeatherFlow–Tempest-fed and excluded; official KCEU and KLQK observations used instead

days.label: Friday
days.precipitation: 5% or less during the day; 60–75% after midnight
days.hazard: No official NWS alerts; northeast gusts near 20 mph develop today and may reach 25–30 mph tonight as rain approaches
days.forecast: Cloudy and cooler beneath a dry cold-air-damming wedge. Northeast winds increase to 7–12 mph, with daytime gusts near 20 mph. Temperatures reach the middle 70s in most locations. Clouds lower tonight, with rain developing after midnight and northeast gusts increasing toward 25–30 mph.

days.label: Saturday
days.hazard: No official NWS alerts at issuance; independent analysis identifies heavy rain, localized flash flooding, patchy fog, northeast-to-east gusts of 30–40 mph and isolated tree or power-line impacts
days.forecast: Cool, cloudy, windy and wet. Rain should be falling across most of the Upstate by daybreak and becomes widespread and heavier during the afternoon and night. Temperatures remain in the 60s beneath the wedge. Rainfall near Clemson may reach 2–4 inches through Saturday night, with 4–6-inch maxima possible closer to favored Blue Ridge Escarpment and headwater locations.

days.label: Sunday
days.precipitation: 75–90% through the afternoon; 10% or less Sunday night
days.hazard: No official NWS alerts at issuance; localized flash flooding remains possible early, followed by a small conditional risk of damaging gusts or a brief tornado as the wedge erodes—greatest east and northeast of Clemson
days.forecast: Rain and embedded thunderstorms continue Sunday morning but should move out faster than earlier forecasts indicated. Southwest flow and a developing dry slot may erode the wedge, allowing temperatures to rebound into the 70s and possibly lower 80s. A small afternoon severe-weather window is possible if instability develops, especially farther east toward the Charlotte area. Mostly clear and dry conditions arrive Sunday night.

upstate.bottomLine: Today remains dry, cloudy and cooler. Rain arrives after midnight and becomes widespread Saturday, with the greatest flash-flooding and wind concerns Saturday afternoon through Sunday morning. Rain exits Sunday afternoon, when a small severe-weather risk could emerge if the wedge retreats quickly enough.
upstate.confidence: High on today's wedge and widespread Saturday rain; moderate-high on the heavy-rain corridor; moderate on Sunday's high and severe potential because models differ on how quickly the wedge and remnant circulation depart

sourceNotes: Official airport observations span 7:15–7:30 AM EDT. Central Kentucky was clear, calm and cool, while official Upstate stations were dry with northeast winds beneath increasing high cloud. No Tempest observations were used.

The NWS point forecasts were generated at 7:44 AM EDT. Louisville's 6:13 AM discussion supports low- to middle-80s warmth today, a 6–12-hour faster Saturday rain arrival, 0.75–1.50 inches area-wide with localized 2.5–3-inch totals, and gusts up to 30–35 mph. Greenville-Spartanburg's 6:45 AM discussion supports a Friday wedge, widespread rain by Saturday afternoon, 4–6-inch maxima near favored escarpment terrain and a small Sunday severe-weather risk.

The NWS active-alert API returned no active alerts for either forecast point at approximately 7:44 AM EDT. This official alert status is separate from the independent discussion of heavy rain, localized flooding, gusty winds and Sunday's conditional severe-weather risk.

Model inventories checked at 7:44 AM EDT showed complete 06Z HRRR through hour 48, 09Z RAP through hour 51, 06Z NAM through hour 84, 06Z NAM 3-km Nest through hour 60, 06Z GFS through hour 384, 06Z GEFS mean through hour 276 and 00Z ECMWF through hour 360. These complete cycles cover the full 72-hour forecast.

College of DuPage radar at 7:35 AM EDT showed both forecast regions precipitation-free. Clean-infrared imagery at 7:36 AM EDT showed extensive tropical cloudiness advancing northward while the deeper rain shield remained to the south.

Short-range guidance now clusters near the NWS Friday highs: lower 80s in Central Kentucky and middle 70s in the Upstate. This resolves yesterday's larger Friday temperature disagreement and removes the need to treat HRRR as a warm Upstate outlier today.

Saturday guidance agrees on widespread rain but retains a large Central Kentucky temperature spread. NAM is near the lower 60s beneath faster rain, while the NWS forecast is near 69°F. The 60–71°F range explicitly represents this onset-time uncertainty.

Sunday global guidance differs on the speed of wedge erosion and system departure. GFS supports roughly 70°F in Central Kentucky and upper 70s near Clemson, while ECMWF is warmer near the middle 70s and lower 80s. Wide Sunday ranges and reduced confidence represent this non-material conflict.

Clemson Weather Network identifies its observations as WeatherFlow–Tempest data. Those observations were excluded, and official KCEU and KLQK observations were used for Upstate analysis and verification.

The forecast-accuracy summary generated at 10:34 AM EDT October 8 was consulted. KDVK lows were adjusted downward using the recommended -2°F correction. Upstate low ranges were widened because KCEU has a recommended +1.5°F correction while KLQK has a recommended -3°F correction. No daytime station correction was applied.

HRRR remains the best overall high-temperature model, while ECMWF has the best limited cold-air-damming score. Weekend ranges were widened because 72-hour coverage is 52.5%, cold-air-damming coverage is 50% and wedge-erosion coverage is 50%. High weekend rain probabilities are consistent with the verified 100% observed frequency in the 81–100% probability bin. This candidate does not modify the repository, forecast archive, website or widget.

appliedAdjustments.details: Shifted the lower portion of overnight ranges downward using KDVK's recommended -2°F low correction; KLEX's low bias remains below the application threshold. No high-temperature station correction was applied. Saturday and Sunday ranges were widened because 72-hour coverage is 52.5% and rain timing strongly controls daytime temperatures.

Widened overnight ranges in both directions because KCEU has a recommended +1.5°F low correction while KLQK has a recommended -3°F correction. HRRR received the greatest weight for today's high, with ECMWF also weighted during the wedge because it has the lowest current cold-air-damming model error. Sunday was widened because wedge-erosion range coverage is only 50%.
